Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 1


The British Empire’s policy of indirect rule in colonial India represented a sophisticated form of administrative control that has been both
praised for its efficiency and criticized for its divisive consequences. Unlike direct rule, which involved wholesale replacement of
indigenous institutions with British administrative structures, indirect rule sought to govern through existing native hierarchies and
traditional authorities. This approach was not merely pragmatic-born out of the vastness of the subcontinent and the limited number of
British administrators-but also reflected a calculated strategy to minimize resistance while maximizing control.


The system operated through a complex web of relationships between British officials and Indian princes, zamindars, and other traditional
power holders. The British Resident, typically stationed at princely courts, wielded considerable influence while maintaining the fiction of
native sovereignty. This arrangement allowed the British to claim legitimacy through traditional sources of authority while ensuring that
real power remained in colonial hands. The princes retained ceremonial functions and limited administrative control over internal affairs,
but foreign policy, defense, and ultimately all significant decisions rested with the British.


However, this policy had profound and lasting consequences for Indian society. By preserving and often ossifying traditional hierarchies,
indirect rule reinforced caste distinctions and communal divisions that might otherwise have evolved or diminished. The British found it
convenient to categorize Indians along religious and caste lines, creating administrative categories that became politically significant. This
taxonomic approach to governance contributed to the crystallization of identities that would later manifest in communal tensions and
ultimately influence the partition of 1947. The policy also created a class of collaborating elites who became dependent on British
patronage, complicating the nationalist movement’s efforts to present a unified front against colonial rule.


(390 words | Adapted from: Cambridge Companion to British Imperial History)

Q 1. The author’s characterization of indirect rule as involving “the fiction of native sovereignty” primarily serves to:

a) Emphasize the complete powerlessness of Indian rulers under British control.

b) Highlight the deliberate deception inherent in the colonial administrative strategy.

d) Illustrate the British respect for traditional Indian governmental structures.

b) Unequivocally condemnatory of its divisive social consequences.

d) Ambivalently torn between its efficiency and its moral implications.


Q 5. According to the passage, the collaborating elite created by indirect rule complicated nationalist efforts because they:

a) Actively opposed independence movements to protect their privileges.

b) Represented a contradiction to claims of unified anti-colonial sentiment.

c) Were more numerous than committed nationalist leaders.

d) Possessed greater legitimacy in the eyes of ordinary Indians.

a) Eliminating ancient social structures through administrative reform.

b) Creating legal protections for historically marginalized communities.

c) Strengthening the authority of traditional rulers within their domains.

d) Making flexible social systems rigid and unchangeable.

Passage – 2


The emergence of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) represents perhaps the most significant evolution in monetary systems since
the abandonment of the gold standard. Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, which operate on decentralized networks and derive their
value from market speculation and network effects, CBDCs are digital representations of a nation’s fiat currency, backed by the full faith
and credit of the issuing government. This fundamental distinction has profound implications for monetary policy, financial stability, and
the very nature of money itself.


The potential benefits of CBDCs are compelling. They could dramatically reduce the costs associated with printing, distributing, and
securing physical currency, while providing governments with unprecedented real-time visibility into economic transactions. This granular
data could revolutionize monetary policy implementation, allowing central banks to adjust interest rates and money supply with surgical
precision based on actual spending patterns rather than lagged economic indicators. Furthermore, CBDCs could extend financial services
to underbanked populations, providing secure, government-backed digital payment systems without requiring traditional banking
infrastructure.


However, the implementation of CBDCs raises profound concerns about privacy, surveillance, and individual autonomy. Unlike cash
transactions, which are inherently anonymous, CBDC transactions would be traceable and recordable by the issuing authority. This
capability could enable unprecedented government surveillance of individual spending patterns, potentially chilling free expression and
political dissent. The programmable nature of digital currencies also raises dystopian possibilities: governments could theoretically
impose expiration dates on money, restrict its use for certain purchases, or even freeze individual accounts instantly based on political or
social criteria.


The international implications are equally complex. CBDCs could challenge the dominance of the US dollar in international trade,
particularly if major economies like China successfully implement their digital yuan for cross-border transactions. This could
fundamentally alter global power dynamics and reduce America’s ability to enforce economic sanctions. Conversely, the network effects

inherent in digital payment systems might create new forms of monetary hegemony, where the first-mover advantage in CBDC
implementation translates into disproportionate influence over global financial architecture.


(430 words | Adapted from: The Economist, “Central Bank Digital Currencies: Promise and Peril”)

Passage – 3


The hard problem of consciousness, as formulated by philosopher David Chalmers, represents perhaps the most intractable challenge in
contemporary philosophy of mind. While neuroscience has made remarkable progress in mapping the neural correlates of consciousness
and explaining the functional aspects of mental processes-what Chalmers terms the “easy problems”-the question of why there is
something it is like to have subjective experiences remains stubbornly resistant to scientific explanation. This explanatory gap between
objective neural activity and subjective phenomenal experience strikes at the heart of our understanding of the relationship between mind
and matter.


The conventional materialist approach assumes that consciousness emerges from complex neural interactions in much the same way
that wetness emerges from H2O molecules. However, this analogy fails to capture the uniqueness of the consciousness problem. While
we can fully explain wetness in terms of molecular behavior without any residual mystery, consciousness presents what philosophers call
the “qualitative” or “phenomenal” aspects of experience-the redness of red, the painfulness of pain, or the taste of chocolate-that seem to
resist reduction to purely physical descriptions. These qualia appear to possess an irreducible subjective dimension that cannot be
captured by objective scientific methodology.


Several theoretical frameworks have emerged to address this challenge. Integrated Information Theory (IIT), developed by Giulio Tononi,
proposes that consciousness corresponds to integrated information (?) in a system, suggesting that any system with sufficient integrated
information will be conscious. This theory makes the counterintuitive prediction that certain artificial systems or even collections of
photodiodes could possess consciousness. Global Workspace Theory, championed by Bernard Baars, focuses on the functional
architecture of consciousness, proposing that conscious experiences arise when information becomes globally accessible across
different brain modules. Panpsychism, increasingly defended by philosophers like Philip Goff, takes the radical step of proposing that
consciousness is a fundamental feature of reality, present even in elementary particles.


Yet each of these approaches faces significant challenges. IIT struggles with its implication that isolated systems could be highly
conscious, potentially leading to a consciousness explosion in complex networks. Global Workspace Theory, while functionally elegant,
doesn’t obviously bridge the explanatory gap between access and phenomenal experience. Panpsychism faces the combination problem:
how do micro-conscious entities combine to create unified conscious experiences? The persistence of these difficulties suggests that our
current conceptual frameworks may be fundamentally inadequate for understanding consciousness, requiring either revolutionary
scientific breakthroughs or radical philosophical reconceptualization.


(430 words | Adapted from: Philip Goff, Galileo’s Error: Foundations for a New Science of Mind)

b) The persistent failure of scientific methods to explain subjective experience.

b) Illustrate the theory’s advantage over competing frameworks.

a) Explain how information becomes globally accessible across brain modules.

b) Account for the functional architecture underlying conscious experience.

c) Bridge the gap between information access and subjective experience.

d) Provide testable predictions about conscious versus unconscious processing.


Q 18. The passage suggests that resolving the hard problem of consciousness may require:

a) More sophisticated neurotechnology to map brain activity.

b) Better integration of existing philosophical and scientific approaches.

c) Fundamental changes in our conceptual understanding.

d) Abandonment of the scientific method in favor of philosophical inquiry.

Passage – 4


She had always been suspicious of happiness, the way it arrived unannounced and settled into the corners of her life like dust that would
inevitably need sweeping away. Margaret watched her daughter Clara arrange flowers in the crystal vase-white roses, baby’s breath,
eucalyptus-with the methodical precision of someone who believed that beauty could be imposed upon chaos through careful attention to
detail. The afternoon light streaming through the kitchen window caught the water droplets on the petals, creating tiny prisms that
scattered rainbow fragments across the marble countertop.


“You don’t have to stay,” Clara said, not looking up from her arrangement. “I know you have your book club.”


But Margaret couldn’t leave, not yet. There was something about the quality of light, the particular way Clara’s hands moved among the
flowers, the almost religious concentration on her daughter’s face that made her want to memorize this moment before it dissolved into

the ordinary succession of minutes that comprised their days. She had learned, after David’s death, that happiness-real happiness, not the
manufactured kind that came in greeting cards and pharmaceutical advertisements-was always borrowed time, always subject to
revocation without notice.


Clara stepped back to assess her work, tilting her head with the same gesture she had made as a child when puzzling over jigsaw pieces
or math problems. The resemblance to David in that moment was so sharp that Margaret felt her breath catch. But instead of the familiar
ache of loss, she experienced something else: a recognition that grief and joy were not opposites but rather different faces of the same
deep capacity for love, different ways of measuring what mattered.


“They’re beautiful,” Margaret said, and meant it in ways that encompassed more than flowers.


Clara smiled-not the careful, protective smile she had worn for months after the funeral, but something genuine and unguarded. “I thought
we might have people over again. Small dinners, nothing elaborate. What do you think?”


Margaret nodded, understanding that this was not really about dinner parties but about Clara’s tentative willingness to reengage with life,
to risk the vulnerability that came with opening one’s door and heart to others. The flowers were not merely decoration but declaration: we
are ready to create beauty again, ready to believe in the possibility of celebration even in the shadow of loss.


The late afternoon sun shifted, and the prisms on the counter scattered into ordinary water droplets. But something had changed in the
quality of the silence between them, something that felt like permission-to hope, to plan, to trust in the reliability of small joys even when
larger sorrows remained unresolved.


(510 words | Original Fiction for CLAT Practice)

Q 24. Which of the following best describes the overall emotional arc of the passage?

a) From protective anxiety to cautious acceptance of future possibilities.

b) From bitter resignation to enthusiastic embrace of new beginnings.

c) From quiet scepticism about happiness to a mature reconciliation of grief and hope.

d) From emotional detachment to sudden overwhelming joy.

US President Donald Trump suggested that Cuba could be the next target of American military action, even as he referred to recent US
operations involving Venezuela and Iran. Speaking at the Future Investment Initiative conference in Miami, Florida, Trump said, “Cuba is
next, by the way-but pretend I didn’t say that. Please, please, please, media, disregard that statement. Thank you very much. Cuba’s next.”
The remarks come after the US military raided Venezuela and forcibly seized its president, Nicolás Maduro, on January 3, and launched
ongoing large-scale joint attacks with Israel on Iran on February 28, according to Xinhua news agency. Cuba has been facing a severe
economic and energy crisis due to decades of US sanctions. The United Nations has warned that fuel shortages are pushing the country
towards a humanitarian crisis. Earlier this month, Trump had said Cuba is likely to “fall pretty soon”, but added that his administration
would focus on Iran “right now”. Trump also sharply criticised NATO, calling it a “paper tiger” and questioning whether Washington should
continue defending allies that, he said, failed to support the United States in times of need. Speaking at the Future Investment Initiative
Priority Summit in Miami, he said the alliance had not backed the US when it mattered. “NATO is a paper tiger… They didn’t come to our
aid,” he said. In unusually blunt remarks, Trump suggested a reassessment of US commitments to the alliance. “Why would we be there for
them if they’re not there for us?” he said, describing NATO’s response as a “tremendous mistake”. He also recounted conversations with
European leaders, including French President Emmanuel Macron, saying offers of support came only after military action had concluded.
“As soon as the war is over, we will send ships,” Trump quoted Macron as saying, adding, “I don’t want them when the war is over.”

Twelve years after the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh, the Rajya Sabha passed the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill,
clearing the way for Amaravati to be officially incorporated as the sole capital of Andhra Pradesh, with effect from June 2, 2024. The Bill
received near-unanimous support across political parties in the Upper House, with the notable exception of the YSR Congress Party
(YSRCP), whose MPs opposed it, arguing that the Bill ignored the demands of farmers in the area. The debate was initiated by senior
Congress MP Renuka Chowdhury, who criticised the 12-year delay, calling it a “statement of national shame” and questioning why it took
so long to fulfil a commitment made on the floor of the House. Union Minister and Telugu Desam Party (TDP) leader K. Rammohan Naidu

welcomed the development, saying it redefined the pride, faith and consciousness of the country in its democracy and leadership. In
essence, the passage of the Bill formally puts to rest years of uncertainty over Andhra Pradesh’s capital following its split from Telangana
in 2014, finally giving the State a constitutionally recognised, single capital city in Amaravati.


When Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy and the YSRCP came to power in 2019, they proposed a controversial Three-Capital Model for Andhra
Pradesh, citing regional balance and financial viability as key reasons. The three capitals proposed were:
• Visakhapatnam as the Executive/Administrative Capital
• Amaravati as the Legislative Capital
• Kurnool as the Judicial Capital


More recently, even as the Amaravati Bill was being passed in Parliament, Jagan proposed that instead of Amaravati, a “capital corridor”
named MAVIGAN should be formed by combining Vijayawada, Guntur, and Machilipatnam. Jagan claimed that the MAVIGUN model could
save up to Rs. 1.9 lakh crore compared to the Amaravati project.

The central government notified a 4 per cent retail inflation target with a tolerance band of 2 percentage points on either side for a five-year
period from April 1, 2026, to March 31, 2031. According to a gazette notification issued by the Department of Economic Affairs under
Section 45ZA of the RBI Act, 1934, the upper tolerance limit has been fixed at 6 per cent, while the lower limit is set at 2 per cent. The
decision has been taken in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), retaining the existing inflation-targeting framework. This
marks the second consecutive extension of the same target, after it was first introduced in 2016 and later continued in 2021. The
framework formally mandates the RBI to maintain inflation around 4 per cent, with flexibility within the 2-6 per cent band. India adopted
the flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework in 2016, with the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), headed by the RBI
Governor, tasked with setting policy rates to achieve this objective. Over the past decade, inflation has remained within the prescribed
band for roughly three-fourths of the time, although volatility increased during the pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Recent data
shows retail inflation rose to 3.21 percent in February from 2.74 per cent in the previous month. The latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) is
based on a revised series with 2024 as the base year. Ahead of this notification, the RBI had released a discussion paper in August 2025
seeking stakeholder feedback on key aspects of the inflation framework. These included whether headline or core inflation should guide
policy, whether the 4 per cent target remains optimal, if the tolerance band needs revision, and whether a fixed target should be replaced
with a range. The RBI noted that the FIT framework has broadly performed well, with inflation averaging around 4 per cent in its early years
and stabilising again in recent years after a spike during global disruptions. It emphasised the need for policy certainty and credibility,
especially amid heightened global and domestic economic uncertainty.

India inducted its third nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN), INS Aridaman, significantly strengthening its sea-based
nuclear deterrent capabilities. The Indian Navy also commissioned the advanced stealth frigate INS Taragiri at a separate ceremony.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh presided over the commissioning ceremonies. The inductions signify a major enhancement in India’s
naval strength and maritime combat capabilities. At the commissioning ceremony of INS Taragiri, the fourth vessel of Project 17A of the
Nilgiri-class stealth guided-missile frigates, Singh said it is a unique platform, as it fits perfectly into every role - from high-intensity combat
to maritime security, anti-piracy operations to coastal surveillance, and humanitarian missions. With INS Aridaman’s induction, India will
have three operational ballistic missile submarines at sea for the first time. The indigenous SSBN is designed to carry more long-range
nuclear-tipped missiles than INS Arihant and INS Arighaat, which were commissioned in 2016 and 2024, respectively. A larger 7,000-tonne
vessel, INS Aridaman will carry more K-15 missiles, as well as the intermediate-range K-4 nuclear-capable submarine-launched ballistic
missiles (SLBM) - with nearly double the number of VLS tubes than its predecessors - that can hit targets 3,500 km away. A fourth SSBN is
currently under construction. India is also pursuing a nuclear-powered attack submarine (SSN) programme. The Navy plans to build two
SSNs indigenously and acquire one on lease from Russia, which is expected to arrive by 2027-28 and bridge the capability gap until India’s
own boats are ready. INS Aridaman will join its predecessors as a key component of India’s nuclear triad, which refers to a country’s ability
to launch nuclear missiles from platforms in the air, land, and at sea. India is part of a select group of countries with nuclear triad
capabilities. These include the United States, Russia and China.

A motion is a formal idea by a member to do something. Its objectives form the basis of the collective decision-making process. It helps to

collectively and members of each House individually, without which they would not be able to discharge their functions efficiently and

Indian citizenship is governed by the Citizenship Act, of 1955, a key piece of legislation that outlines how an individual can become a
citizen of India. With its roots in the Indian Constitution and updated over the years to reflect changing realities, this Act defines five main
ways to acquire Indian citizenship.


Citizenship by Birth: Anyone born in India between January 26, 1950, and June 30, 1987, is automatically considered an Indian citizen,
regardless of the nationality of their parents. For those born on or after July 1, 1987, at least one parent must be an Indian citizen at the
time of birth for the child to qualify as an Indian citizen.


Citizenship by Registration: Persons of Indian origin (PIO) who have been residing in India for at least seven years are eligible to apply. The
required residency period typically includes having lived in India continuously for the 12 months immediately before applying, as well as for
six out of the eight years preceding that period. Foreign nationals married to Indian citizens can apply for citizenship through registration if
they have been married and residing in India for a continuous period of seven years. Minor children of Indian citizens are eligible for
registration without any specific residency requirement. Individuals whose parents are or were Indian citizens are also eligible, even if born
outside India. In addition, persons who or whose parents were residents of undivided India before the partition and who are now residing
in India may qualify.


Citizenship by Descent: Citizenship by descent applies to individuals born outside India. If a person was born between January 26, 1950
and December 10, 1992, they are considered an Indian citizen if their father was an Indian citizen at the time of their birth. However, for
individuals born outside India after December 10, 1992, either parent must have been an Indian citizen at the time of the child’s birth.

Citizenship by Naturalization: To qualify, an applicant must have resided in India for at least 12 months immediately before the date of
application, and for an aggregate of 11 years in the 14 years preceding that 12-month period. The applicant must be of good character,
have adequate knowledge of at least one of the languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, and intend to reside in
India or serve the Indian government.


Citizenship by Incorporation of Territory: When a foreign territory becomes part of India through legal means-such as a treaty, cession, or
political agreement-the Government of India may, by order, specify the conditions under which the people of that territory are granted
Indian citizenship.
